title: Antireflective bilayer metasurfaces with complete wavefront control - Nature Nanotechnology
byline: Oh; Jaewon; Cassara; Davide; Palmieri; Alfonso; Piatti; Lorenzo; Rodrigues; Janderson Rocha; Dorrah; Ahmed H; Dainese; Paulo; Capasso; Federico
html:
Abstract

Antireflection coatings are widely used in optical systems to increase transmission and suppress unwanted reflections by matching the optical impedance across a uniform interface. Applying the same idea to metasurfaces is fundamentally more challenging because their wavefront control relies on arrays of geometrically distinct meta-atoms, presenting as a spatially varying optical impedance. Here we show that vertical integration can overcome this limitation by allowing bilayer meta-atoms to act simultaneously as phase shifters and impedance-matching stacks. By treating meta-atoms as multilayer thin films, we derive a design rule that links the effective refractive indices of two independently patterned layers and identifies antireflective bilayer libraries with full 0–2π transmission phase coverage. We demonstrate the approach with a free-standing TiO2/TiO2 metalens operating at 1,310 nm, which suppresses reflection below that of bare glass while maintaining diffraction-limited focusing. These results establish bilayer metasurfaces as a platform for jointly engineering optical impedance and wavefront response at the meta-atom level.

Main

Metasurfaces shape optical wavefronts using subwavelength scatterers that impart prescribed local responses on incident light1, enabling compact flat-optical components for imaging2,3,4, holography5,6, beam shaping, structured-light generation7,8,9 and fibre-based communications10,11. Their optical throughput is critical because reflection losses reduce the photon budget and generate parasitic back reflections that complicate system integration12,13. Dielectric metasurfaces potentially offer higher throughput due to their low absorption and nearly arbitrary phase control14,15. Improvements in their efficiency have focused mainly on controlling the transmitted field more accurately, via topology16,17,18,19 and shape20 optimization. These approaches substantially enhance wavefront fidelity and diffraction efficiency but do not explicitly eliminate reflection losses.

A complementary route to higher efficiency is to reduce parasitic reflection through antireflective design. In conventional optics, reflection at an interface can be suppressed by impedance matching using a thin-film coating21 (Fig. 1a(i)). Extending this concept to metasurfaces, however, is fundamentally non-trivial, as metasurfaces have a spatially varying reflectivity. Each meta-atom composing the metasurface is obtained from a library of nanopillar geometries with fixed height but varying lateral dimensions. A meta-atom approximates an effective refractive index that determines the phase and amplitude of not just the transmitted light but also the reflected light (Fig. 1a(ii)). A uniform antireflective coating placed on top of a metasurface can then satisfy the impedance-matching condition only approximately and for a narrow range of meta-atoms22,23,24,25,26 (Fig. 1a(iii)). A further limitation is that a top coating suppresses reflections only at the air–metasurface interface, leaving the losses at the metasurface–substrate interface unaddressed. Effective antireflection therefore requires co-design of the entire material stack27 rather than adding it after fabrication. Recent advances in bilayer metasurface fabrication provide a route to address this library-level constraint by embedding antireflection directly into the meta-atom architecture28,29.

A conventional thin-film antireflective (AR) coating (R ≈ 0%; i); a single-layer metasurface without (R ≈ 5%; ii) and with (R ≈ 3%; iii) a conventional antireflective coating; and our free-standing bilayer metasurface (R ≈ 1%; iv). b, Cross-sectional schematic of the bilayer metasurface and corresponding effective thin-film model where light is incident from the top. Each bilayer meta-atom is approximated as two homogeneous films with effective refractive indices n1 and n2 and thicknesses d1 and d2, placed between a superstrate and substrate with refractive indices ninc and nsub, respectively. c, Geometric interpretation of the reflected fields in the complex plane. d, Calculated reflectance of the effective thin-film stack at normal incidence for λd = 1,310 nm, plotted as a function of the effective indices n1 and n2 for fixed film thicknesses. The white solid curve Rmin marks the locus of index pairs that minimize the reflectance for each value of n2. e, Fraction of Rmin values less than –30 dB for each pair of possible film thicknesses d1 and d2.

Here we use two vertically stacked nanopillar layers with independently controlled lateral geometries (Fig. 1a(iv)) and model each bilayer meta-atom as an effective thin-film stack consisting of the incident medium, the two nanopillar layers and the substrate (Fig. 1b). In this picture, each element acts as a local phase shifter and impedance-matching stack. Because the two patterned layers provide independently tailorable effective indices30, the bilayer architecture supplies the degrees of freedom needed to minimize reflections from every interface while preserving the phase coverage required for wavefront shaping. In other words, the metasurface is not impedance matched after the phase library is designed; impedance matching is built into the library itself. Using this framework, we design TiO2/TiO2 bilayer metalenses operating at a design wavelength of λd = 1,310 nm. Full-device simulations show that the bilayer architecture reduces the 5.1% reflectance of a conventional single-layer metalens to 1.2%, effectively eliminating 76% of the total reflection losses. A reflectance well below that of a bare glass substrate is achieved without compromising wavefront manipulation: the bilayer and single-layer devices exhibit nearly identical point-spread functions (PSFs) and Strehl ratios. Because more light is funnelled through the metasurface at no cost of phase error, the focusing efficiency increases. Experimentally, we demonstrate an improvement in the focusing efficiency from 86% for the single-layer control to over 90% for the bilayer metalens with the same aperture and focal length.

Thin-film model of the bilayer meta-atoms

The core objective is to construct a meta-atom library that is both phase addressable and antireflective. A single, patterned layer with fixed height and varying lateral geometry cannot satisfy both requirements across the full 0–2π phase range, because meta-atoms at different phase levels present as different effective indices, so no single impedance-matching condition can be enforced uniformly across the library. The upper-layer geometry supplies the missing degree of freedom that can be tuned independently from the bottom-layer geometry to suppress reflectivity and yield the desired transmitted phase, simultaneously.

The resulting bilayer architecture is approximated by a thin-film model (Fig. 1b). When the response of a subwavelength pillar lattice is governed by their fundamental Bloch mode, the lattice can be represented by a homogeneous medium with an effective refractive index given by the modal propagation constant31,32,33. A bilayer meta-atom is then modelled as a stack of four media with refractive indices ninc, n1, n2 and nsub, where n1 and n2 are the Bloch-mode effective indices of the upper and lower nanopillar layers, respectively, and d1 and d2 are their thicknesses34. The index of the incident medium is ninc and the substrate is nsub.

This description reduces the meta-atom antireflection problem to that of a classical bilayer antireflective coating35,36. We analyse its reflectance with the vector method21; transfer-matrix calculations37 give nearly indistinguishable results (Supplementary Section 1). which gives a simple geometric interpretation of antireflection. In the complex plane, zero reflection is obtained when the reflection vectors that arise from every interface interfere destructively and form a closed triangle (Fig. 1c), with side lengths set by Fresnel coefficients and angles, by phase thicknesses.

This picture also shows why antireflection is difficult to enforce across a library. For each pair of effective indices, exact triangle closure requires unique phase thicknesses δ1 and δ2. A metasurface, however, has fixed d1 and d2 values, so exact closure cannot be enforced for every meta-atom. The thicknesses must instead be co-optimized, so the library as a whole remains weakly reflective.

We apply this design principle to TiO2/TiO2 bilayer meta-atoms on glass, with nsub = 1.447 and ninc = 1, at a design wavelength of λd = 1,310 nm. For a representative thickness pair, d1 = 290 nm and d2 = 1,300 nm, equation (3) gives the reflectance map in effective-index space (Fig. 1d), where each point (n1, n2) represents one possible bilayer meta-atom. Free-standing bilayer fabrication requires the upper TiO2 pillar to be laterally no larger than the lower one, which for the same material constrains n1 ≤ n2 (ref. 38), a limitation that can be relaxed by using stacks of hybrid materials.

Thus, f assigns to each lower layer the upper-layer effective index that best impedance matches the full stack. The resulting minimum-reflectance locus is shown by the white solid curve in Fig. 1d. Repeating this optimization over all viable thickness pairs gives a family of mappings f and corresponding minimized-reflectance curves. The mapping f(n2) is the core result of the thin-film model. Achieving antireflectivity in metasurfaces demands a local design rule rather than just a global coating criterion. For each library element, the upper layer is therefore not a uniform coating, but a phase-level-dependent layer co-designed with the lower layer to impedance match the full meta-atom. Representative reflection-vector plots of select meta-atoms (Supplementary Section 2) confirm the geometric origin of their antireflective response.

Antireflective bilayer meta-atom library construction

The thin-film model defines the target relation between the two layers. We translate this effective-index rule into physical nanopillar geometries using rigorous coupled-wave analysis, implemented with Reticolo39, which directly returns the Bloch-mode effective indices of each periodic structure.

The square cross-section was chosen for polarization insensitivity32. g is a function that maps nanopillar geometry to effective index. The resulting bilayer library (d2 = 1,300 nm, d1 = 290 nm) is compared with a conventional single-layer TiO2 reference (d = 1,300 nm) in Fig. 2d,e. Both libraries provide complete phase coverage, but the bilayer library maintains markedly higher transmittance across the entire set of meta-atoms. In particular, the minimum transmittance increases from 86.7% in the single-layer library to 97.6% in the bilayer library. This library-level improvement suppresses reflection without sacrificing phase coverage and should translate into higher device-level efficiency.

This construction relies on the effective-medium approximation, which holds while the lattice response is dominated by the fundamental Bloch mode. We verified that all meta-atoms in the library operate in this single-mode regime by comparing transfer-matrix and rigorous coupled-wave analysis transmittances40 (Supplementary Section 3).

The framework is not restricted to identical materials in the two layers; an example hybrid TiO2/amorphous-Si (a-Si) design at λd = 1,550 nm is presented in Supplementary Section 4.

Device-level validation of bilayer metalenses

We next evaluate whether the antireflective advantage obtained at the meta-atom-library level is retained in a complete optical device. We compare metalenses designed from the bilayer library with reference metalenses designed from the single-layer library. A representative bilayer metalens designed for λd = 1,310 nm is shown in Fig. 3a, where the focal length is F = 1 mm, diameter is D = 250 μm and numerical aperture is NA = 0.18. The lower TiO2 pillars are shown in green, whereas the upper TiO2 pillars are in blue. A single-layer TiO2 metalens with identical aperture and focal length serves as the reference. We simulated both devices using finite-difference time-domain calculations in Tidy3D (ref. 41), over the full 250 μm aperture. The simulated reflectance spectra are shown in Fig. 3b. At the design wavelength, the reflectance decreases from 5.1% for the single-layer device to 1.2% for the bilayer device, much less than the 3.3% Fresnel reflectance of a bare glass substrate. Equivalently, the bilayer architecture eliminates 76% of the total reflectance of the single layer.

summary: A bilayer meta-atom structure engineers the antireflective capabilities of the metasurface, without affecting its full 0–2π transmission phase coverage.
